# demo-video feature specification

What the demo recorder promises, and the automated test that covers each behavior. The recorder is
dev-only tooling: nothing here is distributed, and nothing it produces is committed.

Run the suite from `.github/skills/demo-video`:

``bash
node --test tests/timeline.test.mjs tests/redact.test.mjs tests/cli.test.mjs
``

The required `validate` CI job runs the same command.

## Scheduling

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEMO-PLAN-01 | A montage is cut to a fixed length, so `planBeats` splits the requested duration across the beats in proportion to their weight and the per-beat budgets sum to it EXACTLY (largest-remainder apportionment, never plain rounding). A beat whose proportional share falls under the `MIN_BEAT_MS` readable floor is pinned to the floor and the remaining time is re-shared proportionally among the beats that are still free, keeping the total on budget. An impossible budget (shorter than the floor times the beat count), an empty beat list, a non-positive/NaN duration, or a fractional duration (whole milliseconds cannot sum to it) throws instead of silently truncating. The beat list is also the demo's contract: ids are unique, every beat declares at least one ability and a `run` step, and the union of declared abilities equals the advertised `REPORT_ABILITIES` - which covers commenting on prose, an image, a code diff, a Mermaid node and a Chart.js chart, because "any content is commentable" is the claim the montage exists to demonstrate. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a beat plan always adds up to exactly the requested duration (DEMO-PLAN-01)`, `weight decides the share, and a floor is funded by the longest beat (DEMO-PLAN-01)`, `an impossible or malformed budget is refused, not silently truncated (DEMO-PLAN-01)`, `the report montage covers every advertised ability (DEMO-PLAN-01)` |
| DEMO-PLAN-02 | A degenerate weight never produces a degenerate plan. `Infinity` divided by `Infinity` is `NaN`, which would spread silently into every budget and every sleep derived from it, so a non-finite, zero, negative or non-numeric weight falls back to 1 exactly like a missing one - the budgets stay whole numbers above the floor and still sum to the request. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a degenerate weight cannot produce a NaN budget (DEMO-PLAN-02)` |
| DEMO-PLAN-03 | The readable floor must itself be a positive whole number of milliseconds. A fractional floor smuggles a fraction into the plan through the back door - the pinned beat keeps it and the budgets no longer sum to the request - so it is refused rather than silently overshooting. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a fractional floor cannot break the exact-budget contract (DEMO-PLAN-03)` |
| DEMO-PLAN-04 | The clip opens on an INTERACTION, not on a still document. Waiting for every diagram and chart to render before the first beat put three seconds of a motionless page at the head of every montage, which reads as a stuck video; a beat that needs a drawn figure declares `needsDiagrams` instead and the wait is taken immediately before that beat, by which point the figure has long since drawn. The opening beat is a required one and starts on the selection affordance a reader discovers first, with the synthetic cursor gliding in (animated in the page, so it costs the beat nothing) rather than teleporting into place. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the montage opens on an interaction and declares its own diagram waits (DEMO-PLAN-04)` |

| DEMO-PLAN-05 | Every beat names itself on screen. A montage moves fast and has no narrator, so a viewer who cannot tell an image comment from a diagram comment learns nothing from either: each beat carries a short caption ("Commenting on a diagram", "Editing a comment", "Exporting for sharing") shown as a toast for its duration. Captions are unique and short enough to read at speed, and they are part of the demo contract rather than decoration. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `every beat names itself on screen (DEMO-PLAN-05)` |

## Fast-forward (idle compression)

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEMO-FF-01 | A real Copilot CLI session is mostly waiting, so `compressTimeline` replays any gap longer than `idleMs` as a short `holdMs` beat flagged `fastForward` (with the skipped duration recorded, which the renderer shows as a badge), while gaps UNDER the threshold are left exactly alone so streaming and typing keep their real rhythm. Events are re-timed, never dropped, reordered or rewritten. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `dead air collapses to a hold and short gaps are left alone (DEMO-FF-01)` |
| DEMO-FF-02 | Compression can only ever shorten: the replayed clock is monotonic, the result never exceeds the source duration, and a threshold above every gap fast-forwards nothing. A hold longer than the idle threshold would EXPAND a gap and is refused, as are a non-positive threshold, non-monotonic timestamps, and a non-array input. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a compressed timeline stays monotonic and never grows (DEMO-FF-02)` |
| DEMO-FF-03 | `fitTimeline` picks the idle threshold whose compressed length is closest to the requested clip length, so a 40 minute session and a 3 minute one both land near the ask, and a session already shorter than the target is never stretched. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `fitTimeline lands a long session near the requested clip length (DEMO-FF-03)` |
| DEMO-FF-04 | Idle thresholds are discrete, so with only a couple of long waits no threshold lands near the target and the clip would waste the budget. Once a threshold is chosen the HOLD is solved for the remaining time - capped at `MAX_HOLD_MS` so a fast-forward stays a beat rather than a stare. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the hold stretches to use the target when few gaps carry the session (DEMO-FF-04)` |
| DEMO-FF-05 | A session whose real length already fits the target is returned UNCOMPRESSED, whatever its gap structure. The candidate list has a ceiling, so without this a single gap longer than the largest candidate was fast-forwarded even when the clip had explicitly been asked to be longer than the session. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a session shorter than the target is never compressed, however long it is (DEMO-FF-05)` |
| DEMO-FF-06 | Candidates are compared by the length they can ACTUALLY achieve, i.e. after each one's own hold is solved - not by their length at the default hold. Choosing first and stretching afterwards picks a threshold another candidate could beat, missing a target it was possible to hit exactly. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `fitTimeline compares candidates by their SOLVED length, not their default one (DEMO-FF-06)` |
| DEMO-FF-07 | The configuration `fitTimeline` REPORTS reproduces the timeline it returns. Computing with a fractional hold while reporting a rounded one meant replaying the reported settings produced a different clip length than the one just handed back. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the fit it reports reproduces the timeline it returns (DEMO-FF-07)` |
| DEMO-FF-08 | "Do not compress at all" competes as a candidate at EVERY target, not only when the session already fits. Short-circuiting it meant a 700 second session asked for 690 seconds came back as a 1.5 second clip - missing by 688 seconds where leaving it alone missed by 10. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a target just under the source keeps the session whole (DEMO-FF-08)` |
| DEMO-FF-09 | The hold moves in BOTH directions within its bounds. Solving only upward meant a session with many gaps could not be brought DOWN to the target - 85 fast-forwards at the default hold is 27 seconds of holds alone, so a 35 second request produced 63. A hold passed explicitly is an instruction, not a starting point, and is honoured exactly. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the hold shrinks as well as grows to hit the target (DEMO-FF-09)` |
| DEMO-FF-10 | The hold can never exceed its cap or its threshold: a cap below the requested hold is a contradiction and is refused rather than silently ignored, a non-finite or negative hold is rejected up front, and the solved hold is floored (not rounded) so it cannot land above a fractional threshold and trip `compressTimeline`'s own guard as an internal error. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the hold can never exceed its cap or its threshold (DEMO-FF-10)` |
| DEMO-FF-11 | Skipped time adds up the same way twice: the reported total is summed from the ROUNDED per-event values, so the figure the render summary prints is the sum of its parts rather than a separately-rounded number that disagrees with them. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `skipped time adds up the same way twice (DEMO-FF-11)` |
| DEMO-FF-12 | Collapsing the waits is not always enough: a TUI redraws constantly, so a long session carries real sub-threshold streaming that no idle threshold touches - a 17 minute panel run still came to 81 seconds against a 40 second request. When even the best fit overshoots, the clip plays at a uniform faster rate, which keeps the rhythm (compressing small gaps further would destroy it) and is how anyone watches a terminal recording anyway. A session that already fits plays at normal speed. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `uniform speed-up lands a busy session on the requested length (DEMO-FF-12)` |
| DEMO-FF-13 | The closing stretch is exempt from that speed-up. The end of a session is usually the whole point - the consolidated summary, the verdict - and racing through it defeats the clip, so `tailMs` marks a span of SOURCE time at the end that replays at its natural pace while the earlier bulk absorbs the compression. Order is preserved across the join. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the closing stretch is exempt from the speed-up (DEMO-FF-13)` |

| DEMO-FF-14 | The OPENING is exempt from the speed-up as well as the ending. The start is where a viewer reads what was asked for and the end is where the answer lands, so both spans replay at their natural pace and the middle - the long stretch of the panel grinding away - absorbs the compression. Order is preserved across both joins. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `the opening is exempt from the speed-up as well as the ending (DEMO-FF-14)` |
| DEMO-FF-15 | Writes that share a moment of the replay are merged. A compressed middle asks the player to write thousands of chunks milliseconds apart, and each write costs real time to parse and paint, so the replay could not keep up and the clip ran ~50% long however aggressive the schedule was. Merging removes that floor without dropping a byte or reordering anything; a fast-forward event is a boundary, so its badge and skipped time stay on the right moment. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `writes that share a moment are merged without losing a byte (DEMO-FF-15)` |
| DEMO-FF-16 | An explicit `--idle` is an instruction, not one candidate among the defaults. Letting the fitter choose whichever threshold lands closest to the requested length quietly defeats a protected head or tail, because that threshold also collapses the gaps INSIDE the protected span - a panel summary meant to play at its natural pace arrived pre-compressed, and the body speed-up had nothing left to give (the middle capped out near 5x when 41x was wanted). A pinned threshold keeps the source pacing intact and pushes all the fitting into the hold and the body speed-up. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a pinned idle threshold is honoured, so a protected tail keeps its pace (DEMO-FF-16)` |
| DEMO-FF-17 | A WINDOW of the finished clip can be re-timed on its own. A review note is almost always local - "seconds 20 to 27 drag" - and re-fitting the whole clip to answer it disturbs the parts that were already right, so `--speed-windows from:to:factor` speeds up exactly that stretch. Windows are given in CLIP time (what the viewer can point at, title card included), must not overlap, and events after one shift earlier by exactly the time it saved - never re-scaled, never dropped, never reordered. A malformed window is refused rather than silently ignored, because a clip that quietly came back at the old pace is the failure this exists to prevent. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a window of the clip can be re-timed without disturbing the rest (DEMO-FF-17)` |

| DEMO-FF-18 | When the protected head and tail between them cover the whole session there is no body left to absorb the compression. Falling through to the uniform speed-up then raced through exactly the spans the caller asked to preserve, silently - and the boundary arithmetic made that case unreachable to detect, because `findIndex` returning -1 means "the head covers everything" at one end and "the tail covers nothing" at the other. The clip now keeps its own pace and reports `protectedOverrun`, because an honest overshoot beats a silently unprotected summary. A genuine body is still fitted. | `tests/timeline.test.mjs` - `a fully protected clip overruns honestly instead of racing its protected spans (DEMO-FF-18)` |

## Redaction (what must never reach a published clip)

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEMO-SAFE-01 | Every built-in credential shape is scrubbed: GitHub tokens (classic, server and fine-grained), OpenAI/Anthropic keys, AWS access key ids, Slack and Google keys, JWTs, `Authorization`/bearer credentials, private key blocks, and keyword-anchored assignments including a prefixed environment variable (`AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET=`) and a connection-string password. Scrubbing is a fixed point: a cleaned line reports no further findings and is unchanged by a second pass, so the render gate cannot be tripped by its own redaction marker. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `every built-in secret shape is scrubbed out of a line (DEMO-SAFE-01)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-02 | Over-redaction ruins a demo, so the rules are anchored on literal markers rather than entropy heuristics: ordinary session output - a git sha, a uuid, a file path, a URL, test output - passes through byte-for-byte and reports no findings. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `ordinary session output is left completely alone (DEMO-SAFE-02)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-03 | The operator's home path and account name are anonymised by rules composed at call time (never baked into the defaults, since they depend on who is recording), on both Windows and posix paths, while the SHAPE of the path is preserved so the clip still reads like a real session. No home or user given, no rules invented - and a home that normalizes to nothing (`/`, as in a container) registers no rule at all, since an empty pattern matches every position and would replace the gap between every character. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `the operator's home path and account name are anonymised (DEMO-SAFE-03)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-04 | A ConPTY hands output over in arbitrary slices, so a credential routinely straddles two chunks and a naive per-chunk scrub would pass both halves through. The streaming scrubber holds back a tail and splits only on whitespace (which no credential shape contains), catching a token cut at any offset while passing a clean stream through byte-for-byte and in order. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a secret split across PTY chunks is still caught (DEMO-SAFE-04)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-05 | `scrubEvents` cleans a whole captured cast before it is written: event count and timings are preserved (only text moves, so the replay keeps the session's rhythm), the number of redactions is reported, and the transcript handed to the human reviewer is exactly the text the clip will show, so review and video can never disagree. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `scrubEvents cleans a whole cast and reports what it found (DEMO-SAFE-05)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-06 | A TUI colourises as it prints, so a credential routinely arrives with ANSI escape sequences INSIDE it - the terminal renders the token perfectly and a viewer reads it straight off the clip, while a byte-level regex sees two harmless fragments. Matching therefore runs against the VISIBLE projection of the text and the redaction is mapped back onto the raw bytes it covers, so a painted token is both scrubbed and reported. Escapes outside a credential are untouched, so the clip keeps its colour. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a token wrapped in ANSI colour codes is still caught (DEMO-SAFE-06)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-07 | A PEM private key is the one credential shape containing whitespace, and its body far exceeds the carry buffer, so a whitespace-split scrubber would emit `BEGIN` in one flush and `END` in another and match neither. The streaming scrubber holds an unterminated block and emits a complete one whole, so `cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519` mid-session is redacted however the PTY chunks it; a block too large to buffer is redacted from its `BEGIN` marker rather than emitted in the clear. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a private key block streams through the scrubber intact (DEMO-SAFE-07)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-08 | Output with no whitespace at all (a minified payload, a long base64 blob) can never be split safely, so past a hard cap the scrubber force-emits to avoid growing without bound. It scrubs the WHOLE buffer before that cut, so the cut can never slice a credential in half and let both halves through, and ordinary output is neither lost nor truncated. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a whitespace-free flood cannot push a credential out unredacted (DEMO-SAFE-08)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-09 | Searching the whole buffer for a split point on every push is quadratic precisely when the stream is densest, which would freeze a recorder mid-session. The scrubber remembers how far back is known to hold no whitespace, keeping the work linear. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `the streaming scrubber stays linear on whitespace-free input (DEMO-SAFE-09)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-10 | A credential the APPLICATION hard-wrapped across two lines has no contiguous byte run to match, but the viewer reads it straight off the screen. Matching therefore runs a second pass over a newline-joined projection, restricted to the rules whose shapes cannot contain whitespace - running the line-oriented rules unwrapped would let `[^\r\n]+` run away and redact the entire clip. Ordinary wrapped prose is untouched. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a token the application wrapped across lines is still caught (DEMO-SAFE-10)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-11 | xterm replays the stream into a GRID, so a replacement shorter than the token it replaced pulls the rest of the line left and visibly breaks a boxed or column-aligned frame. A redaction is padded to the width it replaced; a replacement longer than its match is never truncated, because safety wins over alignment. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a redaction keeps the column width it replaced (DEMO-SAFE-11)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-12 | Escapes are projected by CLASS, because the two kinds pull in opposite directions. A STYLE escape is dropped so a colourised token rejoins and matches; a CURSOR-MOVING or erasing escape becomes a space, because dropping it glues unrelated runs together and destroys the word boundary a token rule needs - `Loading123<CSI 0G>ghp_...` renders as the token overwriting the progress line, yet scanned clean. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a cursor-move escape cannot glue a token past its word boundary (DEMO-SAFE-12)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-13 | A home directory is anonymised by SHAPE (`/home/<name>`, `/Users/<name>`, `C:\Users\<name>`) as well as by the current operator's identity, so a cast captured on another machine - whose owner's name these rules never knew - is still cleaned, without anyone's identity being written into the cast to make it work. The tail of the path survives, so the clip still reads. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a home path is anonymised even for a cast from another machine (DEMO-SAFE-13)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-14 | Overlapping spans are MERGED, never dropped. Two credentials separated only by a newline each produce a span reaching into the other on the unwrapped projection, and skipping the second left its tail in the clip - where, no longer looking like a token, it also passed the gate. Containment is treated separately, so an assignment keeps the key that makes it readable (`GH_TOKEN=[redacted]`) instead of collapsing to one opaque blob. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `two adjacent credentials are both redacted whole (DEMO-SAFE-14)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-15 | A redaction never swallows the line structure around it. A span found on the unwrapped projection straddles the newline the token was wrapped over, so control bytes inside a replaced span are re-emitted in place - otherwise the replay loses a terminal row and everything after it shifts up. Unwrapping is deliberately biased to over-redact: the word immediately after a join may be absorbed, and the rest of the line survives. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a redaction never swallows the line structure around it (DEMO-SAFE-15)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-16 | The PEM markers are located through the same projection as everything else, so a TUI that colourises the header cannot slip past the streaming hold and have the key body flushed line by line into the cast and transcript. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a PEM header wearing colour codes still holds the stream (DEMO-SAFE-16)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-17 | Width padding applies to opaque redactions, not to identity rewrites. Padding a path rewrite to its original width inserts a space inside the path (`/home/demo /.ssh/config`), which reads as two tokens and looks broken in a clip whose whole point is to look right. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `an identity rewrite is not padded into a broken path (DEMO-SAFE-17)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-18 | EVERY OSC escape is stripped from the stream, not just the window-title forms. The projection consumes the whole body of any OSC sequence and projects it to a space, so no rule can match inside one - while the raw bytes still reach the cast and the transcript. A shell reports its working directory in OSC 7 and a hyperlink target (which can carry a URL password) rides in OSC 8, and both are emitted by default, so both were invisible to the gate. The replay has no use for any of them; visible link text survives. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `the terminal title escape never reaches the cast (DEMO-SAFE-18)`, `every OSC escape is stripped, not just the title (DEMO-SAFE-23)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-19 | Past the buffer cap an oversized private key stays SUPPRESSED until its END marker arrives. Emitting a redaction and forgetting the block was still open let every byte after the cap through as ordinary text, with no BEGIN marker left for the gate to recognise; output after the key resumes normally. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `an oversized private key stays suppressed to its END marker (DEMO-SAFE-19)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-20 | A line break is a safe place to flush unless it is the JOIN of a hard-wrapped credential - credential characters pressed against it on both sides. Splitting there flushed the first half before the unwrapped pass could see the whole token, so a continuation longer than the carry buffer kept its tail. Such a join is skipped when choosing the split, and the character class spans base64 and URL-safe values (`+`, `/`, `=`, `%`, `~`), not just identifiers. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a wrapped credential longer than the carry keeps no tail (DEMO-SAFE-20)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-21 | A rule whose VALUE half cannot contain whitespace also runs over the unwrapped projection, so an assignment or a bearer credential the application wrapped mid-value is caught whole. Without it the keyword matched on the first line and the continuation stayed in the clip with nothing keyword-shaped left to catch it. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a wrapped assignment value does not leave its tail behind (DEMO-SAFE-21)` |
| DEMO-SAFE-22 | Scrubbing is idempotent however the marker is punctuated. A session that DISCUSSES redaction quotes it (`'Authorization: [redacted]'`), and demanding whitespace after the marker made the header rule re-match its own output - so the render gate refused a cast this very tool had already cleaned. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `scrubbing is idempotent however the marker is punctuated (DEMO-SAFE-22)` |

## Scripted capture (driving a session unattended)

A demo has to be re-recordable on demand, and the loop clip needs a session with TWO turns and a long
browser phase in between. So the turns are declared in a file rather than typed by hand.

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-01 | A script is validated up front, not half-run: it needs a non-empty `steps` array, every step needs a unique `mark` (marks are how a render finds a turn in the cast), exactly one of `send`/`sendFile`, a non-empty `expect` if given, and non-negative numbers. A step with no explicit condition gets a default quiet window; one with an `expect` or `expectFile` does not, because an agent that is streaming its answer never goes quiet first. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `a script is validated up front rather than half-run (DEMO-SCRIPT-01)` |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-02 | A step waits for quiet, for a marker in the output, or for a FILE to appear - and the timeout is always the backstop, reporting rather than throwing so a capture that ran long still yields the session it did record. Waiting on a file is what lets one session span the browser phase: the capture sits on the prompt until the review bundle the montage produces exists on disk. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `a step waits for quiet, a marker, or a file, and the timeout is the backstop (DEMO-SCRIPT-02)` |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-03 | An OPTIONAL step is skipped when it times out rather than sent blind. The folder-trust dialog appears once per machine and never again, so a required step would fire its keystroke into whatever is on screen instead - typically the prompt, corrupting the very turn the clip is about. Without this the script only works on a fresh machine, which is the opposite of re-recordable. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `an optional step is skipped on timeout, not sent blind (DEMO-SCRIPT-03)` |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-04 | A file-backed step is READ at send time, not at parse time, so parsing succeeds while the file is still absent. In the loop capture the review bundle is produced by the browser phase, which runs long after the script was parsed; a missing file at send time is a clear error naming the step and the path. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `a file-backed step is read at send time, not at parse time (DEMO-SCRIPT-04)` |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-05 | Enter is a SEPARATE write, after a pause. A TUI composer that receives a long string and a trailing carriage return in one burst treats the return as typed text: the prompt lands in the composer and simply sits there, which is how a fifteen minute capture produced no session at all. A multi-line step is sent as a real bracketed paste, with CRLF normalized first, or every newline submits its own turn. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `Enter is a separate write, and a paste is bracketed (DEMO-SCRIPT-05)` |
| DEMO-SCRIPT-06 | A script that cannot be used says which file and why - missing, or not valid JSON - rather than failing later inside a session that is already running with a pty attached. | `tests/script.test.mjs` - `readScript reports the file it could not use (DEMO-SCRIPT-06)` |

| DEMO-SAFE-24 | A credential broken across a hard wrap is caught even when the emulator brackets the break with an erase or cursor escape - the shape a real TUI actually emits. Mapping every movement escape to a space (so unrelated runs can never be glued into one apparent token) also split the token in the projection whose whole job is to rejoin it, so the token matched nothing, scrubbed to nothing, and the gate reported ZERO findings while both halves stayed legible in the clip. A run of adjacent escapes containing a newline and flanked by token characters is now dropped whole; any other movement escape still becomes a space, which is what preserves the anti-gluing guarantee. | `tests/redact.test.mjs` - `a credential wrapped with an erase or cursor escape at the break is still caught (DEMO-SAFE-24)` |

## Command line and the safety gate

| Feature id | Behavior | Covering tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DEMO-CLI-01 | `report --list` reports the plan for the montage without launching a browser: the requested length, the example it will drive (which must exist on disk), the `.webm` it will write, and per-beat budgets that sum exactly to the request. | `tests/cli.test.mjs` - `report --list prints a plan that sums to the requested length (DEMO-CLI-01)` |
| DEMO-CLI-02 | The argument contract fails loudly instead of guessing: an unknown option, a repeated option, an option given no value, a non-positive number, an unknown subject, an option belonging to a DIFFERENT subject, and a missing example all exit non-zero with a message naming the problem. Silently ignoring any of them means recording something other than what was asked for. | `tests/cli.test.mjs` - `the argument contract fails loudly rather than guessing (DEMO-CLI-02)` |
| DEMO-CLI-03 | The safety gate is on by default and fails FAST - before a browser is launched. `scan` and `render` both read the cast's COMMAND as well as its output, so a credential passed on the command line cannot be waved through, and a missing cast file is an error rather than an empty render. A clip rendered over the gate's objection is named `UNSAFE`, including when the caller supplied the filename. | `tests/cli.test.mjs` - `the safety gate refuses a dirty cast before any browser starts (DEMO-CLI-03)` |
| DEMO-CLI-04 | A Windows shim is launched through its interpreter. Resolving `copilot.cmd` on PATH is only half the job: node-pty cannot spawn a `.cmd`/`.bat`/`.ps1` directly, so the documented `capture -- copilot` flow failed for the shims most CLIs install as, even with the file sitting right there. A real executable is still launched directly, and nothing is wrapped off Windows. | `tests/cli.test.mjs` - `a Windows shim is launched through its interpreter (DEMO-CLI-04)` |

## Coverage gaps

These are deliberate, and are covered by review rather than by a test:

- **The clips themselves.** Whether a montage reads well, whether a beat filmed the right thing, and
  whether anything sensitive is visible are judgements about pixels. The tool supports the judgement
  (`scan` for the cast, `frames` for the clip) but cannot make it. Every capture is reviewed by a
  human before it is published.
- **What no rule can know.** Repo contents, paths, branch and issue text, error messages and stack
  traces, other people's names and email addresses from git history, hostnames and org identifiers,
  and credential shapes no rule matches. These are documented in SKILL.md as the operator's job
  rather than pretended away, because a false sense of coverage is worse than none.
- **Terminal semantics beyond the stream.** The scrubber reads bytes; the viewer reads the rendered
  grid. A credential typed with a backspace, or drawn out of stream order by a full-screen TUI, is
  reconstructed only on screen. Closing that would mean emulating a terminal to scrub one, which is
  disproportionate; it is documented as a limitation instead.
- **Browser and PTY driving.** The beat steps, the xterm replay page and the node-pty capture need a
  browser, a native module and a live command, so they are exercised by running the tool (which is
  the whole point of an ad-hoc recorder) rather than by CI. Everything reachable WITHOUT those - the
  scheduling, the compression, the redaction, and the whole command-line and gate surface - is
  covered by the tests above.
